content:
Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation that develops after an infection elsewhere in the body, usually a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or a bowel infection such as food poisoning. It often affects the knees, ankles or feet, and can also cause sore eyes and pain when weeing. Most people recover fully within a few months to a year.

What causes it

The joint itself is not infected. Instead, the immune system overreacts to an infection somewhere else and starts attacking healthy tissue in the joints. Common triggers include:

  • chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections
  • bowel infections such as salmonella, campylobacter or shigella, often from food poisoning

Symptoms usually start between one and four weeks after the infection, and sometimes the original infection caused few symptoms. It is most common in young adults. A gene called HLA-B27 makes it more likely.

Symptoms

Joints and tendons

  • pain, swelling and stiffness, often in the knees, ankles or feet
  • usually affects a few joints rather than many, often on one side
  • heel pain or a swollen "sausage" finger or toe
  • lower back or buttock pain

Eyes

  • red, sore or sticky eyes (conjunctivitis)
  • less commonly, uveitis: a painful red eye with blurred vision and light sensitivity. This needs same-day assessment.

Urinary and genital

  • pain or burning when weeing, needing to wee often, or discharge

General

  • tiredness, a mild fever, and sometimes skin rashes or mouth ulcers

Diagnosis

Your GP will ask about recent infections, including stomach upsets and sexual health. There is no single test. You may have blood tests to check for inflammation, urine or swab tests for infections, and sometimes fluid taken from the joint. Testing joint fluid helps rule out septic arthritis, a joint infection that needs emergency treatment.

Treatment

  • Treating the trigger infection. If an STI such as chlamydia is found, antibiotics will be given, and partners should be tested and treated. Sexual health clinics are free and confidential.
  • Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) are usually the first treatment for joint pain and swelling.
  • Steroid injections into a swollen joint, or steroid tablets, may be used if NSAIDs are not enough.
  • DMARDs such as sulfasalazine or methotrexate may be offered by a rheumatologist if symptoms last longer than six months.
  • Eye drops for eye inflammation, arranged by an eye specialist if needed.

Looking after yourself

  • rest a very painful joint during a flare, then start gentle movement as it settles
  • use cold packs for swollen joints and warmth for stiffness
  • a physiotherapist can help you regain strength and movement
  • pace activity, as fatigue can last for a while

Recovery

Most people get better within a few months to a year. Some have symptoms that come back, and a small number develop long-term arthritis. If symptoms last more than six months, ask about a rheumatology referral.

Reducing the risk of it happening again

Use condoms with new partners, get tested for STIs, and follow good food hygiene. If you have had reactive arthritis before, mention it if you get another infection.

Work, sport and everyday life

During a flare you may need time off work or a break from sport. A fit note from your GP covers longer absences. As the swelling settles, return to activity gradually. Low-impact exercise such as swimming or cycling is often easier on sore knees and ankles than running. Most people are able to return to their usual activities once the inflammation has gone.

If you feel low or anxious while recovering, which is common with any painful condition, talk to your GP. Support is available, and you do not have to wait until you feel at breaking point to ask.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
